summary: Chabad (Chabad-Lubavitch) is the intellectualist school of Hasidism founded by Shneur Zalman of Liady (1745-1812), the Alter Rebbe, whose name is an acronym of Chochmah, Binah, and Da'at (wisdom, understanding, and knowledge), the three intellectual sefirot. On the school's account the mind, through sustained contemplation of the divine, is the disciplined route to love and awe of God and to cleaving to Him (devekut), the intellect generating and governing the emotions rather than emotional arousal alone; this is the descriptive distinction Chabad draws with the affective piety it labels 'Chagat' (Chesed-Gevurah-Tiferet) in the wider Hasidic world. Its foundational text is the Tanya, its leadership passed as a dynasty of rebbes associated with the town of Lubavitch, and in the twentieth century it became known for a wide programme of outreach (shlichus).
description:
Chabad, more fully Chabad-Lubavitch, is a school and movement within Hasidism founded by Shneur Zalman of Liady (1745-1812), the Alter Rebbe, a disciple of Dov Ber the Maggid of Mezeritch, in the region of White Russia (Belarus) at the end of the eighteenth century. Its name is an acronym, ChaBaD, of Chochmah (wisdom), Binah (understanding), and Da'at (knowledge), the three uppermost, intellectual sefirot, and this naming carries the school's distinctive emphasis. The account that follows presents the school's teaching as its own attributed teaching rather than as claims the editor affirms or denies.

What the scholarship and the school itself identify as distinctive of Chabad is the place it gives to the mind. Where the affective Hasidism traced to the Baal Shem Tov and the Maggid's wider circle is characterized as turning on the arousal of emotion and on self-annihilation before the divine, Chabad as Shneur Zalman shaped it makes the intellect the disciplined path to devekut (cleaving to God): the mind, through sustained contemplation (hitbonenut) of the divine, is to generate and rule the emotions (the middot), so that love and awe of God arise from understanding rather than displacing it. Within the movement this is drawn as a contrast between the ChaBaD path, working from the three intellectual faculties, and a 'Chagat' path, named for the emotional sefirot Chesed, Gevurah, and Tiferet, ascribed to mainstream Hasidism; the distinction is recorded here as the school's descriptive self-understanding and is not an evaluation ranking one path above the other. Neither the intellectualist path of Chabad nor the affective piety of other Hasidic courts is presented here as the correct or superior form of Hasidic devotion.

The foundational text of Chabad is the Tanya (Likutei Amarim), first printed by Shneur Zalman in 1796, which sets out the doctrines the school studies as authoritative: the two souls of every Jew (an animal soul and a divine soul 'truly a part of God above'), the beinoni (the 'intermediate' person) as the attainable ideal, and the ten faculties of the soul divided into the three intellectual powers (chochmah, binah, daat) and the seven emotional attributes, corresponding to the supernal sefirot. Scholars of the school, among them Naftali Loewenthal, describe its emergence as a project of 'communicating the infinite', the rendering of an esoteric contemplative mysticism into a teaching that a broad community could study and internalize.

Leadership of Chabad passed after Shneur Zalman as a dynasty of rebbes, the successive heads of the movement, and the line became associated with the town of Lubavitch (in present-day Russia), from which the movement's fuller name Chabad-Lubavitch derives; the seventh and last rebbe of the main line was Menachem Mendel Schneerson (1902-1994). In the twentieth century Chabad-Lubavitch became widely known, factually as a matter of the movement's organized activity, for an extensive programme of outreach to other Jews, its emissaries (shluchim) establishing Chabad houses and institutions across the world under the banner of shlichus ('emissaryship'). This entry presents Chabad on the tradition's own terms as the intellectualist school of Hasidism founded by Shneur Zalman, with its teachings attributed to the school and its founder and with the scholarship recorded alongside, and it adjudicates none of the doctrines it records.
editorial_notes: This entry presents Chabad (Chabad-Lubavitch) on Judaism's own terms as the intellectualist school of Hasidism founded by Shneur Zalman of Liady, the Alter Rebbe (neutrality #1, #4, #6). The school's DISTINCTIVE emphasis, the intellect (Chochmah-Binah-Da'at) as the disciplined route to love and awe of God and to devekut, whereby the mind generates and governs the emotions rather than emotional arousal alone, is stated throughout as the school's OWN ATTRIBUTED teaching ('this naming carries the school's distinctive emphasis', 'as its own attributed teaching', 'as Shneur Zalman shaped it') and is DESCRIBED, not affirmed or denied. The Chabad/Chagat (Chesed-Gevurah-Tiferet) distinction is recorded as the school's DESCRIPTIVE self-understanding and EXPLICITLY not an evaluation: 'the distinction is recorded here as the school's descriptive self-understanding and is not an evaluation ranking one path above the other', and 'Neither the intellectualist path of Chabad nor the affective piety of other Hasidic courts is presented here as the correct or superior form.' The dynastic leadership (the rebbes, Lubavitch, Schneerson as the seventh rebbe) and the twentieth-century outreach (shlichus, shluchim, Chabad houses) are stated FACTUALLY and briefly as matters of the movement's organized activity, not evaluated. period.note: Chabad was founded by Shneur Zalman of Liady (1745-1812) in the last quarter of the eighteenth century in White Russia (Belarus); c. 1775 is an approximate marker for the period in which, after the death of his teacher the Maggid of Mezeritch (1772), he began to lead a Hasidic centre of his own and to shape the Chabad approach (the Tanya was first printed in 1796). The movement continues to the present as an active worldwide movement, so no end date is given; the dates mark the founder's period, not a precise foundation year.

relations.note: Chabad was founded by Shneur Zalman of Liady, the Alter Rebbe (1745-1812), a disciple of the Maggid of Mezeritch; the shneur-zalman entry exists and records the reciprocal 'founded' edge to chabad, naming the ChaBaD acronym and the intellectualist path.

Chabad is one of the enduring branches of the Hasidic movement, its intellectualist school; described as distinct in its emphasis on the mind (ChaBaD) rather than the emotions (Chagat), with the distinction recorded as descriptive and not evaluative. The hasidism entry exists.

The Tanya (Likutei Amarim, first printed 1796) is the foundational text of Chabad, studied within the movement as its authoritative statement of doctrine (the two souls, the beinoni, the intellectualist ChaBaD path). The tanya entry is authored in the same batch.

On Chabad's account the intellect (contemplation, hitbonenut, through chochmah-binah-daat) is the disciplined path to devekut, cleaving to God, the mind generating and governing the emotions; stated as the school's attributed teaching. The devekut concept exists (data/concepts/judaism/devekut.json).

Chabad grounds its system in the Kabbalah, and the Tanya invokes Cordovero's Pardes Rimonim and 'the Kabbalah of the Arizal' (Luria), the contractions of the light of Ein Sof through the vessels of Chabad in the world of Atzilut (Tanya, Likutei Amarim 2, read on open Sefaria). The kabbalah entry exists.

Chabad presents its teaching as a continuation of Lurianic Kabbalah (the Arizal), the clothing of the En Sof light through the vessels, applied to the inner life of the mind (Tanya, Likutei Amarim 2). The isaac-luria entry exists.

sources.citation: Shneur Zalman of Liady. Tanya (Likutei Amarim; Part I also titled Sefer shel Beinonim, 'the Book of the Intermediate Man'), Part I, chapters 1-3; first printed 1796. Open Hebrew and English text on Sefaria (Kehot Publication Society edition). Cited as the openly-auditable primary text of the school, read line-by-line and verified verbatim: chapter 1 opens from the oath (Niddah 30b) 'Be righteous and be not wicked... in your own eyes regard yourself as if you were wicked' and lays out the beinoni (the intermediate); chapter 2 teaches 'The second soul of a Jew is truly a part of God above'; chapter 3 sets out the soul's ten faculties 'corresponding to the supernal ten sefirot', the soul 'divided in two, sechel (intellect) and middot (emotional attributes)', the intellect comprising chochmah (wisdom), binah (understanding), and daat (knowledge) (chabad), which carries the ChaBaD acronym firsthand. These lines were read and verified verbatim as the load-bearing text for the school's intellectualist path and its foundational doctrines.

sources.citation: Loewenthal, Naftali. Communicating the Infinite: The Emergence of the Habad School. Chicago Studies in the History of Judaism. Chicago: University of Chicago Press, 1990 (ISBN 0226490459 / 9780226490458; 336 pp.). The standard academic study of the emergence of the Chabad (Habad) school, treating Shneur Zalman's project of rendering an esoteric contemplative mysticism into a teaching communicable to a broad community (its 'communication ethos'), the intellectualist path to devekut, and the school's leadership; cited as the academic-historian lens on the school. Verified to exist and be on-topic (University of Chicago Press / BiblioVault record; full text on the Internet Archive), not read line-by-line; carries the same medium rating it holds in shneur-zalman.json and tanya.json.

Verified to exist and be on-topic (University of Alabama Press record; Journal of Religion and AJS Review notices), not read line-by-line; carries the same medium rating it holds in shneur-zalman.json and tanya.json.
